guide.summary: AP Research students must read scholarly studies critically: understand their structure, interpret basic statistics and qualitative findings, and judge whether conclusions follow from the method and data.

sections.heading: Reading a study
sections.body: Most empirical articles follow IMRaD: Introduction (question and literature), Method (participants, materials, procedures, analysis), Results (findings without interpretation), and Discussion (interpretation, limitations, future research). Read the abstract for an overview, then the method to judge credibility before trusting the results. Ask: Who were the participants, and how were they selected? Were groups comparable? What exactly was measured, and how? Is the conclusion limited to what the design can support? In the mindfulness abstract, the schools were not randomly assigned, so differences between schools (teachers, demographics, other programs) could explain the results.

sections.heading: Quantitative basics
sections.body: Descriptive statistics summarize data (mean, median, standard deviation). Inferential statistics test whether results are likely due to chance: a p-value below .05 is conventionally called statistically significant, meaning a difference this large would be unlikely if there were no real effect. Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance; effect size shows how big the difference is (here, a 5-point difference on a 60-point scale). Correlation measures association (r from −1 to 1) but doesn't establish causation; confounding variables may explain both. Random assignment in experiments is what allows causal claims; quasi-experiments with pre-existing groups support weaker conclusions. Validity asks whether a measure captures what it claims to; reliability asks whether it is consistent.

sections.heading: Qualitative basics
sections.body: Qualitative research (interviews, focus groups, observations, open-ended responses, document analysis) explores meanings and experiences. Researchers code data, labeling segments with categories, and identify themes across participants. Quality is judged by trustworthiness: clear procedures, rich description, triangulation (using multiple data sources), member checking (confirming interpretations with participants), and reflexivity (acknowledging the researcher's own perspective). Qualitative findings are not meant to generalize statistically, but they can reveal processes and perspectives that numbers miss. Mixed-methods studies combine both to answer different parts of a question.

sections.heading: Worked example: reading a results table
sections.body: A study reports that students who received tutoring improved test scores by an average of 8 points (SD = 10), compared with 3 points (SD = 9) in a control group, with p = .01 and an effect size (Cohen's d) of about 0.5. The p-value indicates that a difference this large would be unlikely if tutoring had no effect. The effect size of 0.5 suggests a moderate, practically meaningful effect. If students were randomly assigned, the study supports a causal claim; if not, other factors such as motivation might explain the difference. Always check sample size, assignment method, and how scores were measured before trusting a conclusion.

sections.heading: Reading qualitative findings
sections.body: Qualitative studies report themes supported by quotations from participants. Judge their quality by asking how participants were chosen, how many were interviewed, whether the researchers explained their coding process, whether they used triangulation or member checking, and whether they reflected on their own perspective. A strong qualitative study offers rich descriptions that help readers understand experiences, even though it does not aim for statistical generalization.

sections.heading: Exam connection
sections.body: In the literature review and oral defense, you will need to explain why you trust or question particular studies. Practice summarizing each key study's method, findings, and limitations in two or three sentences.

sections.heading: Going deeper
sections.body: Be cautious with statistics in popular media. News articles may report that something 'doubles the risk' without giving the baseline: doubling a 1 in 10,000 risk is very different from doubling a 1 in 10 risk. Distinguish relative risk from absolute risk, check sample sizes, and look for the original study when possible. These habits help you evaluate sources for your literature review and explain your own results accurately to non-expert audiences in your presentation.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know IMRaD, descriptive and inferential statistics, p-value, effect size, confounding variable, random assignment, validity, reliability, coding, theme, triangulation, and reflexivity.

sections.heading: Practice habit
sections.body: Each week, read one empirical article and write a short summary of its question, method, sample, findings, and one limitation.

keyTakeaways: Read the method before trusting the results.
Validity = measures the right thing; reliability = consistently.
commonMistakes: Treating p < .05 as proof of a big effect.
Accepting causal conclusions from non-random groups.
Judging qualitative studies by sample size alone.
examTips: In your literature review, note each key study's method and limitation.
In the oral defense, be ready to explain any statistic you report.
guide.cramSheet:
**IMRaD:** Intro · Method · Results · Discussion

**Quant:** mean/SD · p < .05 · effect size · correlation r · random assignment → causation · quasi-experiment · confound

**Measures:** validity · reliability

**Qual:** coding · themes · triangulation · member checking · reflexivity

**Mixed methods:** both

vocab.definition: The standard structure of empirical articles: Introduction, Method, Results, Discussion.
A result unlikely to occur by chance if there were no real effect, often p < .05.
A measure of how large a difference or relationship is.
A factor that affects both variables, providing an alternative explanation.
Placing participants in groups by chance so the groups are comparable.
A comparison using pre-existing groups without random assignment.
Whether a study or measure captures what it claims to.
Whether a measure produces consistent results.
Labeling qualitative data segments with categories.
A pattern of meaning found across qualitative data.
Using multiple data sources or methods to check findings.
A researcher's reflection on how their perspective shapes the research.

practice.stimulus:
Practice abstract (written by Klutch; the study is fictional)

This study examined whether a school-based mindfulness program reduced test anxiety. Ninth graders at two high schools participated. Students at School A (n = 120) received ten weekly 30-minute mindfulness sessions; students at School B (n = 115) continued their normal schedule. Test anxiety was measured with a validated self-report scale before and after the program. School A students' anxiety scores decreased by an average of 6 points on a 60-point scale, compared with 1 point at School B (p = .03). The authors conclude that mindfulness programs reduce test anxiety and recommend adoption in all high schools.

practice.prompt: Critique the study described in the abstract.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Write a conclusion the evidence supports.

rubric.description: Identifies real strengths (validated scale, pre/post measures, comparison group, reasonable sample).
Identifies key weaknesses (no random assignment, self-report, two schools, possible expectancy effects).
States a conclusion the evidence does support.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Strengths: it used a validated anxiety scale, measured anxiety before and after, included a comparison school, and had over 100 students per group.

B. Weaknesses: schools weren't randomly assigned, so other school differences could explain the result; self-reports could be influenced by students knowing they were in a program; and two schools can't represent all high schools.

C. Supported conclusion: at School A, students in a mindfulness program reported larger decreases in test anxiety than students at a comparison school, suggesting the program may help and should be tested in a randomized study.

practice.prompt: Redesign the mindfulness study to support a stronger causal claim.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe how you would assign participants.

rubric.description: Randomly assigns students (or classes) to conditions within the same school(s).
Uses an active control (e.g., study-skills sessions) to address expectancy effects.
Adds a non-self-report or follow-up measure and explains why.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Randomly assign ninth graders within the same schools to the mindfulness program or a comparison group, so school differences are balanced.

B. Give the comparison group an equal amount of time in a study-skills session, so any difference isn't just due to receiving attention or expecting improvement.

C. Add a measure beyond self-report, such as heart rate during a practice test, and a follow-up survey three months later to see whether effects last.

practice.prompt: A student reports: 'My survey of 50 students found that students who play sports had higher GPAs (mean 3.4 vs 3.1, p = .04). This proves that sports improve grades.'

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain the error in the conclusion.

rubric.description: Correctly interprets the mean difference and p-value.
Explains the causal error and gives a plausible confounding variable.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Athletes averaged a GPA 0.3 points higher, and p = .04 means a difference this large would be unlikely if there were no real difference in the population sampled.

B. The survey is correlational: students weren't assigned to play sports. Confounds such as eligibility rules requiring minimum grades, family income, or time management skills could explain both.

C. In this sample, students who played sports had a modestly higher average GPA than those who did not, a statistically significant difference; the survey cannot show whether sports cause higher grades.

practice.prompt: A student interviewed eight first-generation college applicants about the application process and wants to analyze the transcripts.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe how to code and find themes.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe two ways to make findings trustworthy.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain a reflexivity concern and how to address it.

rubric.description: Describes a clear coding process (initial codes, refining, themes).
Names at least two strategies (member checking, second coder, triangulation, audit trail).
Explains how the researcher's own position could shape interpretation and how to address it.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Read all transcripts, assign initial codes to meaningful segments (e.g., 'confusion about financial aid,' 'reliance on siblings'), group similar codes into categories, then identify themes that appear across most participants, recording each decision in a codebook.

B. Ask a classmate to code two transcripts independently and compare; share themes with participants to check accuracy; and compare interview themes with school counseling data.

C. If the researcher is also a first-generation applicant, they might notice experiences matching their own and overlook others. They should note their assumptions before coding and actively look for disconfirming examples.
